name: HCG and clomiphene for voice

lead: hCG and clomiphene are prescription drugs that raise the body's own testosterone, used for fertility and, off-label, for male low testosterone. Forum users mention them hoping higher testosterone will deepen or maintain a lower voice.

hCG mimics luteinizing hormone and stimulates the testes to make testosterone. Clomiphene blocks estrogen feedback in the hypothalamus, increasing GnRH, LH and FSH release. Encyclopedic sources describe no effect on adult voice pitch, and no published studies have tested either drug for voice. Voice deepening from testosterone is associated with puberty, and the laryngeal changes of puberty are generally described as lasting.

paras: Both are prescribed by clinicians for fertility or hypogonadism, with blood-test monitoring. Voice is not a prescribed use.

Clomiphene can cause visual disturbances, headaches and hot flashes, and hCG carries cautions for several conditions. Both are prescription-only in the US, UK and Australia and are banned in competitive sport.

angle.text: hCG and clomiphene are prescription drugs that raise the body's own testosterone, and forum users mention them hoping for a deeper voice. Both are used for fertility and off-label for male hypogonadism; no studies address voice.

lead: In looksmaxxing discussion, human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) and clomiphene (clomifene) are two prescription drugs sometimes mentioned as ways of raising the body's own testosterone, with the idea that higher testosterone could support a deeper, more masculine voice and a more masculine overall presentation. Both are used medically for fertility and, off-label, for male hypogonadism.[1][2]

hCG is a hormone that resembles luteinizing hormone and stimulates the Leydig cells of the testes to make testosterone.[2] Clomiphene is a selective estrogen receptor modulator that blocks estrogen feedback in the hypothalamus, increasing GnRH, FSH and LH release.[1] Its enclomifene isomer works in a similar way and has been studied in secondary hypogonadism.[3] Encyclopedic sources on these drugs describe fertility and testosterone uses and do not describe an effect on adult voice pitch.[1][2][3]

No clinical studies of either drug for voice were found. Voice deepening is a pubertal effect of testosterone on the larynx, and voice problems that persist after puberty, such as puberphonia, are typically treated with voice therapy; hypogonadism is described as something to rule out in some cases.[4]
infobox: Novarel, Pregnyl, Profasi, Ovidrel and others[2]
Prescription-only in the US, UK, Australia[1]
Both appear on anti-doping prohibited lists[1][2]

paras: Clomiphene was synthesised by Merrell chemists in 1956, patented in 1959 and approved in the US in 1967 as Clomid for inducing ovulation in women. It was also studied for advanced breast cancer from 1964 to 1974 but set aside over concerns about desmosterolosis with long-term use. It is on the WHO Essential Medicines List.[1]

The drug is a mix of about 62 percent enclomifene, which is pro-androgenic, and 38 percent zuclomifene, which is pro-estrogenic. It acts mainly in the hypothalamus, where it blocks estradiol's negative feedback and so increases GnRH pulses and FSH and LH release. It is a prodrug whose active metabolites are processed through CYP2D6, so response varies between people; the overall elimination half-life is about 4 to 7 days, and zuclomifene can be detected in urine for months after stopping.[1]

It is also used off-label in men with low testosterone. Wikipedia reports one trial in which testosterone rose from 309 to 642 ng/dL over three months, and says purified enclomifene is reported to raise testosterone about twice as effectively as the mixture.[1] Its use in gynecomastia is less effective than tamoxifen or raloxifene, partly because of the estrogenic isomer.[1]

Reported adverse effects include reversible ovarian enlargement in women, visual disturbances, headaches and hot flashes; rarer effects include liver inflammation, raised triglycerides and reversible hair loss. Contraindications include pregnancy and liver problems.[1]

Enclomifene is the (E)-stereoisomer of clomifene, roughly 62 percent of the clomifene mixture, while the other isomer, zuclomifene, is more estrogenic and can lower testosterone. Enclomifene was investigated for male hypogonadism under the tentative names Androxal and EnCyzix; studies in secondary hypogonadism reported increased total and free testosterone and, in a 2013 comparison with testosterone gel, higher sperm counts. In January 2018 the EMA's CHMP recommended refusing marketing authorization for secondary hypogonadism, and development was discontinued for all indications in April 2021.[3]

hCG is a 237-amino-acid glycoprotein of about 36.7 kDa made by placental trophoblast cells. Its alpha subunit matches that of LH, FSH and TSH, and its unique beta subunit with a carboxy-terminal peptide gives it a longer half-life.[2] In men it stimulates Leydig cells to produce testosterone, and it is used clinically to treat certain forms of hypogonadism, to maintain fertility and testicular size in men on testosterone therapy, and to trigger ovulation in women.[2]

Wikipedia notes that people also use hCG during and after anabolic steroid cycles to help preserve testicular size and natural testosterone production, since steroids suppress the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis and hCG mimics LH.[2] Prolonged use in males can increase androgen production, caution is advised in people with heart failure, hypertension, kidney dysfunction, migraines or epilepsy, and in prepubescent teens it carries a risk of early sexual development and premature growth-plate closure.[2]

The hCG weight-loss diet started with Albert Simeons's 1954 book Pounds and Inches. In 1976 the FDA required a disclaimer on hCG weight-loss advertisements, a 1995 meta-analysis found no scientific support for hCG in obesity, and in 2011 the FDA and FTC moved to pull unapproved over-the-counter hCG products from the market.[2]

Proponents in appearance communities reason that raising endogenous testosterone while avoiding testosterone replacement could support a deeper voice. The Wikipedia articles on these drugs list fertility, hypogonadism and testicular function as the uses and do not mention voice effects.[1][2][3] No published trial was identified that measured vocal pitch or resonance in adults after either drug.

Puberphonia is a functional voice disorder in which a high, falsetto-like voice persists after puberty, usually beginning between ages 11 and 15 and most often diagnosed in males. It is usually psychogenic, and treatment is mainly direct voice therapy with a speech-language pathologist lasting one to two weeks, with surgery for therapy-resistant cases; the article notes only that hypogonadism should be ruled out when the thyroid laminae have not fused.[4]

No studies found on hCG or clomiphene for voice. Studies of enclomifene in secondary hypogonadism are summarized above and examined testosterone and sperm outcomes.[3] Clomiphene's testosterone effect in men is described in a trial summarised on Wikipedia, which reported the rise from 309 to 642 ng/dL over three months.[1]

Both drugs require a prescription in the US, UK and Australia, and both appear on anti-doping lists; clomiphene is banned by WADA under its hormone and metabolic modulators category.[1] Athletes sanctioned for hCG include Manny Ramirez (50-game MLB ban, 2009), Brian Cushing (4-game NFL ban), Dennis Siver (2014) and Jurickson Profar (80-game suspension, March 2025).[2] Clomiphene can appear in black-market products and has been detected in athletes who ate eggs from hens given the drug.[1]

On T Nation, a member with a young teenage voice, no visible Adam's apple and low testosterone discussed his bloodwork on testosterone therapy, illustrating how voice, secondary sex characteristics and low testosterone come up together.[5] Threads on secondary hypogonadism discuss fertility-preserving approaches to low testosterone.[6]

timeline.event: Albert Simeons publishes Pounds and Inches promoting hCG for weight loss.[2]
Clomiphene approved in the US as Clomid.[1]
FDA bans over-the-counter hCG diet products.[2]
EMA committee recommends refusing marketing authorization for enclomifene in secondary hypogonadism.[3]
Enclomifene development discontinued for all indications.[3]
